anime.say: Everyone says I'm fine. And everyone hears that you learned English from a textbook. Let's fix that.

lines.text: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
Then what do people really say?

anime.say: Hey Yuki, how are you? I'm fine, thank you, and you? Wow, very robot. Then what do people really say?
The answer native speakers use every single day? Not bad!
So next time, try: not bad, thanks. Pretty good, you? Or my favourite, can't complain. Which one will you use today?

archival-doc.say: For centuries, English had no dictionary at all. No rules for spelling. No list of words. Here is how that changed.

events.label: Caxton brings the printing press to England
events.subject: building

events.label: Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall, the first English dictionary
events.subject: portrait

archival-doc.say: In 1476, Caxton brings printing to England. In 1604, Cawdrey publishes the first English dictionary. In 1755, Samuel Johnson's dictionary arrives. And in 1828, Noah Webster gives America its own.

props.headline: The Oxford Dictionary Is Complete
props.subhead: Seventy years after the work began, the final part of the great dictionary is printed
props.subject: crowd
props.caption: A dictionary decades in the making

archival-doc.say: Then, in 1928, the Oxford English Dictionary is finally complete. It took about seventy years.

props.title: One New Word a Day
props.subtitle: Three hundred and sixty five words a year
props.subject: landscape

archival-doc.say: They spent seventy years collecting words. You only need one new word a day. Comment the word you learned today.

ink-anatomy.say: Your English is not a talent. It is a muscle. And muscles only grow one way.

props.myth: You need a talent for languages

ink-anatomy.say: Myth: you need a talent for languages. Fact: daily practice is what builds fluency.
Here is the workout. Shadow a podcast for five minutes. Read out loud for five minutes. Write three sentences. And learn one new word.

props.label: minutes a *day*
props.sub: short and daily beats long and rare
props.title: The *magic* number

ink-anatomy.say: Fifteen minutes a day beats two hours once a week. Start today, and save this workout.

map-reveal.say: It started on one small island. Today, you can hear it on every continent.

Number five, England, where it all began. Four, the United States. Three, Nigeria, where English is the official language. Two, Singapore, one of four official languages. And number one, Australia, with its very own accent.
Altogether, about one point five billion people speak English, more than any other language on Earth.
And the next speaker on this map? That is you. Follow to keep learning.

props.title: The Day English Changed
props.subtitle: One battle that rewrote a language

painted-history.say: One morning in 1066, a battle in England changed the words you speak today.
On the fourteenth of October, the Norman knights charged up the hill at Hastings. By evening, King Harold was dead, and England had a French speaking king.

events.label: French becomes the language of power
Thousands of French words enter English
English returns to the law courts
Henry IV takes the throne in English

painted-history.say: For three hundred years, the rulers spoke French. Thousands of French words poured into English. Then, slowly, English came back, to the courts in 1362, and to the throne in 1399.

props.title: Cow or Beef?
props.subtitle: English farmers raised the cow. French lords ate the beef.

painted-history.say: That is why we say cow and pig for the animal, but beef and pork for the meat. The farmers spoke English. The lords spoke French.

pictogram.say: Afraid to speak English? Follow these rules. Do not skip one.
When you make a mistake, keep talking. Do not stop and apologise. Nobody is counting your mistakes.
The daily protocol. Talk to the mirror. Record your voice. Listen back. And never wait until you are perfect.
Rule number three. Do not translate in your head. Think in simple English. Follow for rule number four.

stick-figure.say: What if you stopped translating, and started thinking in English? Here is what happens.
Translating is slow and tiring, and you freeze in the middle of a sentence. Thinking in English is fast, and the words just come.

props.title: What if you tried it for a week?

panels.caption: Day one: name things around you.
Day three: describe what you do.
Day seven: you dream in English.

stick-figure.say: Day one, name the things around you. Cup, door, coffee. Day three, describe what you are doing. By day seven, you might even dream in English.

items.text: Narrate your day in your head

stick-figure.say: Start tonight. Name ten things in your room. Narrate your day in your head. And stop translating every word. Try it, and tell me in the comments.
